Dama, ‘house,’ is a word that occurs several times in the Rigveda. It denotes, according to Roth, the place in which a man wields uncontrolled power (from the root dam, ‘control’).
Foot notes i. 1, 8; 61, 9; 75, 5; 143, 4; ii. 1, 2, etc.; Vājasaneyi Saṃhitā, viii. 24.
St. Petersburg Dictionary, s.v. But this seems very doubtful in view of the apparent connexion of and , ‘build,’ in Greek.

Dam-pati denotes ‘the master of the house’ in the Rigveda, but is more often used in the dual to designate ‘the master and the mistress,’ an expression that may legitimately be deemed to show the high status of women at the time of the Rigveda. See strī.
Foot notes For the form, cf. Macdonell, Vedic Grammar, p. 37, n. 9. Pischel, Vedische Studien, 2. 307 et seq., argues in favour of the spelling daṃpati (adopted by Geldner in his ṛgveda, Glossar). Cf. patir dan. Rv. i. 149, 2; Oldenberg, Sacred Books of the East, 46, 176, 177.

Dāman, a ‘rope’ or ‘girdle,’ is often mentioned in the Rigveda and later. Reference is made to the rope of the sacrificial horse, as well as to the practice of tying calves with ropes. The word occurs in the sense of a ‘band’ of horse hair in the Śatapatha brāhmaṇa.
Foot notes Originally ‘bond,’ from dā, ‘bind.’
